segments.text: Scaling AI in the wild. Please welcome
Philip Kelly.
Hey everyone. Before we get started,
first off, thank you so much for being
here today. I cannot tell you how many
times in my career I've walked into a
giant room full of chairs like this one
and seen like 10 people there and two of
them are my co-workers. So, I really
appreciate everyone being here and
spending 20 minutes together today. What
we're going to talk about today is
inference. And I believe that inference
is the most important technical problem
of the AI wave that we're undergoing
right now. So by way of introduction,
I'm Philip and I work on inference
infrastructure with these awesome people
at base 10. Uh these are a bunch of my
friends. This picture is actually a year
ago. I've got like a hundred new friends
now since this picture was taken. Um,
and what we're working on is basically a
combination of supporting AI native
companies and scaleups and enterprises
with inference for open-source models,
for custom models, for fine-tuned
models. What we're going to talk about
today is the rise of these AI native
companies and not just, you know, the
headline making companies you might have
heard of, but also AI products within
existing companies and within larger
enterprises that are taking off at an
unprecedented rate.
From there, we're going to talk a little
bit about open- source models and how
they've become begun to offer
state-of-the-art capabilities. Finally,
we're going to talk about some of the
challenges of productionizing inference.
And I'm going to talk you through a few
case studies of companies that we've
helped overcome these challenges.
So, the first trend that I want to talk
about here today is the rise of AI
native companies. So, AI native
companies are scaling super fast. the on
Twitter and LinkedIn what everyone's
talking about is how many months did it
take me to get to $100 million ARR to
500 million to a billion how quickly can
I get that decacorn round the growth is
absolutely incredible and the craziest
thing is what's powering that growth is
generally very small teams these AI
native companies or in many cases AI
native products within a larger company
are going to be built and scaled and
sold old with many fewer people than
were needed in previous generations. So
really lean teams are building very
large products.
Here's some examples of these AI native
companies who we've worked with on this
process. Uh you have awesome companies
like Open Evidence who's building a sort
of chat GPT for doctors. You have
companies like Dscript that I use every
day building new interfaces for video
and audio editing off of these AI
models. And what's really cool about all
of these companies is that scale that
they're able to achieve very very
quickly.
But what do they care about during that
journey? What makes their AI products
better in a way that captures that kind
of audience and that kind of market? The
four things that AI native companies
generally care about is number one
quality. Quality is everything in AI
engineering. So much of our entire field
is built around the idea of improving
quality. So you want to use, you know,
fine-tuned models. You want to use
custom models. You want to do good
context engineering. You want to make
sure your evals are in place so that you
know whether or not your product's
getting better or worse with each
iteration. And inference has a little
bit to do with quality. But inference
engineering, if AI engineering is mostly
about quality, inference engineering is
about everything else. We want to make
the product fast. We want to make the
product affordable or we want to make
sure we have positive unit economics.
And we want to make sure that the
product is differentiated across
multiple axises. So what these AI native
companies are doing, they're building
really high quality products off of
these open-source custom models. They're
getting very low latency for real-time
use cases. We're seeing latency targets
in the hundreds of milliseconds in many
cases. They're taking control of their
unit economics and they're using that to
build a differentiated product
experience that's able to compete in
this rapidly growing market.
And the second trend that's powering a
lot of this is the rise of open-source
models. Two or three years ago, I would
not have bet that I would be standing up
on stage in front of you all talking
about inference. Back then it looked
like maybe three or four foundation
model labs and three or four
hyperscalers might need to have people
who know what inference is and know how
to do it to power APIs that the rest of
the industry consumes today. That's
simply not the case. There are this
slide actually I had to send my slides
in a little bit ahead of time. Um so as
a fastmoving industry this slide's
already out of date. We are over 2
million models on hugging face. So you
have more than two million open source
models to pick from if you can run
inference yourself within your company.
You're not limited to those handful of
models from Hyperscalers and Foundation
Labs. You can build your own
intelligence.
And what's especially impressive over
the last year and has unlocked this
trend even further is how open-source
models are now state-of-the-art. They're
offering frontier performance on all
different modalities. Everyone likes to
talk about LLMs. I love LLMs. They're
incredibly powerful. We have awesome
LLMs in the open source domain like GLM,
Quen, DeepSeek, Llama, GPT, OSS. And we
also have great models in other domains.
So Quen image just came out. That's a
great image generation and image editing
model in the in that domain. You have
models like WAN 2.2 which do great video
generation. You have embedding models to
power your rag, your search, your
retrieval. You have transcription models
like whisper, speech synthesis models
like Orpheus TTS. No matter what you're
trying to build, there is an open source
model out there that can do the job and
do it well if you're able to run it
effectively in production.
And what's really cool is the
compounding effect that this trend of
open source models has. For example,
Orpheus TTS, which is in many ways the
number one open-source texttospech
model, has a backbone on Llama 3.2 3B.
So, this is a open source large language
model that Meadow released about a year
ago that then another lab was able to
take adopt to their needs and release a
new model in a completely different
modality. Or if you look at the rise of
embedding models, embedding models are a
place where open source makes a ton of
sense because these models are small,
they're fast, and they're really high
quality with the backbone of these
midsize language models.
But this introduces a new challenge.
Before your path to production was to
just grab an OpenAI API key, or I don't
want to pick on them directly, you know,
it could be an anthropic key, it could
be a Gemini key. you're getting your
your intelligence from a single
centralized provider. But today, if you
want to leverage this trend, you need to
scale up inference and do so quickly so
that you can get to market fast and
capture this massive growth. And you
need to do it cost-effectively so that
you're actually seeing savings from
adopting these models.
So what are the problems of inference?
What are the engineering challenges that
you're going to need to overcome if you
commit to this journey?
Well, what most people start with is
they start with getting some GPUs and
they start with an off-the-shelf
inference engine like VLM or SG Lang or
Tensor RTLM. They put the inference
engine on the GPU. They put the endpoint
on the internet and they say, "All
right, we have production inference.
Let's launch." Doesn't go very well. So,
let's talk about why not. Again, what we
care about is quality. We care about
latency. We care about economics. We
care about differentiation. All of these
things are impacted by inference. On the
quality side, we have to make sure we're
running the model at a high fidelity. If
we're doing something like quantization,
it needs to be done very carefully so
that we don't destroy the quality we've
worked so hard to create. on latency out
out of the box. These inference engines
are not necessarily going to be
configured specifically for your use
case to give you the absolute maximum
performance at whatever throughput
target you need to hit. And you know, if
you're hitting those latency targets,
you need to make sure that you're doing
it in a way that's still cost effective.
And all of this together is what's going
to differentiate the application.
So doing all of these are hard. And you
know, even if you figure it out,
remember we're going from 1 million to
100 million ARR as a company or as a
product faster than ever with teams that
are smaller than ever. So it's not just
about figuring that this out once. It's
about figuring it out over and over
again. Every time you scale to that next
level, add another zero behind the
revenue. Add another zero behind the
user count. So all of these get harder
with scale. some of these challenges.
How are you going to guarantee a low P99
time to first token? How are you going
to keep that guarantee when you spike to
high volume? Are you going to be able to
scale up additional GPUs and have that
high availability? Are your engineers
equipped to make these decisions and to
build these products? Do you have
observability to understand what's going
wrong because things will get wrong? And
then even if you're able to build all of
this, are you able to build it fast
enough that if you spend three or six or
12 months building this out, are your
competitors already scaling to tens or
hundreds of thousands of or tens or
hundreds of millions of revenue on their
product while you're trying to figure
out tooling? So it's a very challenging
thing and let's talk about three
examples of companies who have been able
to overcome these challenges.
So the first story that I want to tell
here today is one of instant
autocomplete. I'm a developer. I type
pretty fast. I can type maybe 45 to 60
words per minute if I really get going.
I imagine there's plenty of people in
the audience here who can type even
faster than that. So, if you're typing
along, you're writing some code and you
want autocomplete suggestions to help
you move even faster. Those suggestions
have to come so quickly. So, if you're
going to build a code completion model,
you need this model to respond as fast
as an engineer can type. That's very
fast.
So, here's an example of a customer we
worked with. Uh, this is Source Graph,
by the way. Um, they wrote a wonderful
blog post about all the work we did
together. And you can see on the uh the
left, oh, that's not the the button.
That's the button. You can see on this
half of the graph before an optimization
was rolled out, you're looking at
latencies of 4 to 600 milliseconds. Now,
the human response time, it varies from
person to person. I have pretty bad
response time. I know I have pretty bad
response time because I've been doing
martial arts my whole life. So, every
time that that my bad response time uh,
you know, shows up, I get punched in the
face and I get reminded that my reaction
time is not that good. But the average
reaction time is about 200 milliseconds.
So, if you want your product to feel
very instant, like you don't want there
to be a perceivable lag between the user
taking an action and the product
responding, 200 milliseconds is a great
target to aim for. And you can see here
before before the optimizations we were
at two to three times that target. After
the optimizations were rolled out were
able to get down to in many cases close
to that 200 millisecond line. So what
happened to to to make that possible?
What are these so-called optimizations
that we're rolling out?
The most important principle of AI
engineering. If you take nothing away
else away from this talk, I'm going to,
you know, embed this number one thing 13
minutes deep so that the people on
YouTube who have already left don't get
it. Only you guys get it. Um, the most
important principle of AI engineering is
that the more constraints that you can
introduce to the problem, the better
performance you're going to be able to
achieve. Code completion is a highly
constrained problem. So when we're
trying to improve our time to first
token or our time to completion for this
code completion model, we have a lot of
constraints. We know that our context is
going to be repeated over and over again
from request to request. We know that
our completion sequence is going to be
very short. We're doing code completion.
We're not writing entire pages of
software. So we're taking in perhaps
tens or you know thousands or tens of
thousands of input tokens but we're only
generating a handful of output tokens.
That's a constraint. Another constraint
is we're working in code. Python or Ruby
or Rust all of these languages that
you're writing have a very small syntax
compared to the entirety of human
language. So with these constraints in
mind, we're able to identify
optimizations to achieve this target.
some of the optimizations here. Number
one is less constraint oriented. We've
just switched to tensor RTLM which is
generally our favorite runtime. It's by
NVIDIA. It generally offers the best
performance. But the the spec the
constraintspecific optimizations were
number one a real focus on KV cache
reuse. So if you want to do prefix
caching, which is taking the first piece
of each request and making sure that you
can pull from a cache and skip the
prefill step every time you want to
process the same input over and over
again, which you have to do a lot with
code completion, we're able to do that.
We're able to implement KV cache reuse.
Uh we're able to do prefix caching and
accelerate many of those requests. The
second constraintbased performance
optimization that we were able to put in
here was adding something called engram
decoding. So what what engram engram
decoding or engram speculation looks
like is you build a dictionary as you do
your prefill. So basically you take a
token and then you take the sequence
that comes after that token and you can
use these later sequences from the
dictionary to speculate as to the
potential output of the next step of the
model. The reason this works is again we
are very constrained in our vocabulary.
Here we're writing code. Code has open
and close brackets. It has a few common
functions. It has parentheses and closed
parenthesis. It has colons. death, pass,
whatever. There's so many different
things in code that are repeated
throughout a codebase. So, with this
look ahead or with this engram decoding,
we're able to, you know, look ahead in
our generation a little bit, pull up,
you know, as many as 30 tokens ahead of
where we're currently generating and
then create those in one big batch
without an expensive forward pass
through the model. It's less important
to take away from this talk that there
are these two specific optimizations for
code completion unless you happen to be
doing code completion in which case come
find me afterwards and we'll note out
all about it. The important thing to
take away from this story is that if you
can introduce some very import some very
clear constraints into your problem
you're going to be able to achieve this
kind of performance speed up. If you're
trying to build a, you know, more
general case, it's much more difficult
to achieve huge jumps in performance.
So again, performance is great, but what
really matters is performance at scale.
So here's a story about a customer who
called us up um and said, "Uh, hey, you
know, we're doing a big launch. How many
GPUs do you have?" That's a question
that, you know, no one no one ever
really likes getting uh because you have
to pull them from all different kinds of
places. And uh fortunately our answer in
this case was able to be well how many
GPUs do you need? Let's talk about this
chart right here because it represents a
way to achieve scale in the AI industry
and that is multicloud. So every single
one of the colors you see in this chart
is a different region in in multiple
different cloud providers and everything
on the Yaxis here is a single Nvidia
H100 GPU. So if you look at this chart,
this charts over the course of a single
day. We're scaling from a couple hundred
GPUs up to over 1,800 and then back down
elastically. What makes that possible?
How are you able to get this much scale
when in many cases the individual
regions of a data center that you're
looking at are simply not going to have
that many GPUs physically racked up
available for you to use. So the answer
is building something called multicloud
capacity management. And if you're
building a largecale production
influence service, you're going to have
to build this because you're going to
need to access GPUs on more than one
cloud. You're going to want to build
some kind of global control plane. And
this this control plane is going to be
able to dispatch the workloads to
different clouds. And within that,
you're going to need to create a bunch
of different workload planes in
different regions, different
geographies, different clusters,
different availability zones. This
provides a lot of value. It's a ton of
work to set up. It took us well over a
year for our infrastructure engineers to
to build this kind of system, but it's
incredibly valuable for a bunch of
reasons. Number one is reliability. It
gets you options like active passive and
active active reliability where if one
cloud provider goes down or one region
goes down, you can fail over to another
one. If there's, you know, a major
outage that lasts for hours, your
product is not really affected. And then
the other one is it gets you more
capacity. You're able to access GPUs
from multiple different providers. You
have a lot more leverage when you're
talking about, you know, making sure
that you get good pricing. And with this
you're able to in a very advanced
version of the system basically treat
every single GPU in the world as a
fungeible resource that you can swap
between at will. So this is the second
important system to build and it points
to the second sort of key optimiz or key
theory of inference engineering and that
is the more scale that you operate at
the more techniques are available to
you. something like this and the
reliability and cost that it introduces
is is not really something that you can
build if you're just using one or two
GPUs to serve a small amount of traffic.
But if you're serving a ton of different
models to a ton of different users, it
makes sense to start building
optimizations like these.
The final story I want to talk about is
invisible bottlenecks. This one's
particularly close to my heart. So I
get, you know, a support ticket or
something along these lines every so
often that basically says, "Hey, Philip,
you wrote this blog post explaining this
highly optimized system with the runtime
with the performance optimizations at
the scale of this multicloud system and
I built it. I set it up and you said it
could run in 200 milliseconds. I'm
seeing 300 milliseconds. You're a liar."
And the answer is uh no, fortunately I
don't think I am. uh the the issue is
oftentimes in that last mile the client
code bottlenecks. So all of this
inference engineering and AI engineering
stuff is new and it's really exciting. I
have a lot of fun working on it. But we
can't let this take us away from the
traditional software engineering that is
also very very important for building
extremely large products at very high
scale very quickly. So some examples of
the kind of bottlenecks that often times
come up in client code is number one
sessions. Establishing a session takes a
couple dozen milliseconds. You want to
reuse that session over and over again
as much as you can. If you're running a
bunch of client requests through a
single system, you might be limited by
the global interpreter lock in Python if
you're just sending a bunch of requests.
Um because you know these high
concurrency systems can hit bottlenecks
if for example you're doing a task like
taking a billion documents and embedding
all of them because you're building a
corpus for rag or you're going to pre
you're building a data set to do a
pre-training model run. So in these
cases, it's important to not only look
at your model runtime, not only look at
your infrastructure, but also look at
your client code and make sure that the
entire system from end to end is
optimized. So scaling AI in production,
it comes down to three principles.
Number one, the more constraints that
you can introduce in your product, the
the better performance you can achieve.
Number two, the more scale you're
operating at, the more techniques and
the more optimizations are available to
you. And number three, I haven't gotten
to this one yet, um, but the the more
that you can do at runtime, the more
that you can modify your system so that
it dynamically adjusts to changing
traffic, not only adjusting the number
of GPUs you're serving on, but adjusting
the parameters that you're passing into
your influence engine, adjusting the
techniques you're using, adjusting,
let's say, in disagregation, the number
of prefill and decode workers that you
have active, the more that you're able
to do at runtime, time rather than
statically at deploy time, the better
that your system is going to be able to
scale both through the daily
fluctuations of a product and also
through the week and monthlong trend
lines that are taking you up and to the
right as everyone wants to go. So in
summary, inference is more than just
GPUs. Inference is one-time
optimization. Inference is
infrastructure optimization. Inference
is even good oldfashioned software
engineering on the client.
Thank you so much for coming through to
the talk. Again, I really appreciate
everyone being here. It's amazing to
look out over so so many people. Uh
definitely follow me on Twitter, follow

I'm posting about these kind of topics

10 booth until about 6:00. So, come
through. It's uh right over that way.
Come through, hang out, and we'll talk
